steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our computer vision paper on HyperHuman, a framework for generating hyper-realistic, controllable human images with diffusion models. Cover why human image generation is hard, the limits of earlier generative models and of structure-controlled diffusion methods, our dataset and two-module design, and end with a summary of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Importance of human image generation; earlier VAE/GAN methods; diffusion models and their failure on human anatomy
- Structural control methods (ControlNet, T2I-Adapter, HumanSD) and their limits
- Our framework HyperHuman: key insight, HumanVerse dataset, Latent Structural Diffusion Model, Structure-Guided Refiner
- Contributions (three-fold)

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation and earlier methods
  - hyper-realistic human images from user conditions (text, pose); applications: image animation (cite), virtual try-on (cite)
  - many efforts on controllable human image generation
  - early: VAEs, reconstruction manner (cite); GANs for realism (cite)
  - some high-quality (cite), but unstable training, limited capacity -> small, low-diversity datasets
  - diffusion models (DMs) (cite): new paradigm, predominant in Generative AI (cite)
  - T2I models Stable Diffusion (cite), DALL·E 2 (cite) still fail on coherent anatomy (arms, legs) and natural poses
  - reason: human articulated, non-rigid deformations; structure hard to describe with text
- Structural control
  - ControlNet (cite), T2I-Adapter (cite): learnable branch modulating pre-trained DMs, plug-and-play
  - feature discrepancy main vs auxiliary branch -> inconsistency control signal (pose maps) vs image
  - HumanSD (cite): body skeleton into diffusion U-Net by channel-wise concatenation; but artistic style, limited diversity
  - only pose; no depth / surface-normal
  - prior work: single control signal or separate independent guidance; no multi-level correlations appearance <-> structure
  - realistic human generation with coherent structure unsolved
- HyperHuman
  - unified framework, in-the-wild human images, high realism, diverse layouts
  - insight: human image structural over multiple granularities, coarse body skeleton -> fine spatial geometry; capture correlations explicit appearance <-> latent structure in one model
  - HumanVerse: 340 M in-the-wild images; annotations: body skeletons, depth, surface-normal, captions, attributes
  - Latent Structural Diffusion Model: pre-trained backbone denoises RGB, depth, normal simultaneously; replicated layers as structural expert branches; handle different domains, spatial alignment
  - appearance, spatial relationship, geometry jointly modeled; branches complementary (structural awareness + textural richness)
  - improved noise schedule against low-frequency leakage (monotonous depth/normal); same timestep per branch
  - Structure-Guided Refiner: compose predicted conditions, high resolution
  - robust conditioning scheme against error accumulation in two-stage pipeline
- Contributions
  - 1) HyperHuman framework; HumanVerse with pose, depth, surface normal; one of earliest human generation foundation model attempts
  - 2) Latent Structural Diffusion Model; Structure-Guided Refiner for better quality, higher resolution
  - 3) experiments: state-of-the-art, hyper-realistic human images in diverse scenarios

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Generating hyper-realistic human images from user conditions, e.g., text and pose, is very important for various applications, like image animation and virtual try-on. So many efforts have explored the task of controllable human image generation. Early methods either use variational auto-encoders (VAEs) in a reconstruction manner, or improve realism using generative adversarial networks (GANs). Some of them create high-quality images, but the unstable training and limited model capacity restrict them to small datasets with low diversity. The recent emergence of diffusion models (DMs) set a new paradigm for realistic synthesis, and they have become the predominant architecture in Generative AI. However, exemplar text-to-image (T2I) models like Stable Diffusion and DALL·E 2 still have trouble creating human images with coherent anatomy, e.g., arms and legs, and natural poses. The main reason is that a human is articulated with non-rigid deformations, and this needs structural information that text prompts can hardly describe.

To get structural control for image generation, recent works like ControlNet and T2I-Adapter add a learnable branch that modulates the pre-trained DMs, e.g., Stable Diffusion, in a plug-and-play manner. But these approaches suffer from feature discrepancy between the main branch and the auxiliary branch, which leads to inconsistency between the control signals (e.g., pose maps) and the generated images. To address this, HumanSD inputs the body skeleton directly into the diffusion U-Net by channel-wise concatenation. However it is limited to generating artistic style images with limited diversity. Also, human images are synthesized only with pose control, and other structural information like depth maps and surface-normal maps is not considered. In short, previous studies either take one control signal as input condition, or they treat different control signals separately as independent guidance, instead of modeling the multi-level correlations between human appearance and the different types of structural information. Realistic human generation with coherent structure is still unsolved.

- HyperHuman: unified framework; insight: structure over multiple granularities (body skeleton -> spatial geometry), model appearance + latent structure together
- HumanVerse: 340 M images; skeletons, depth, surface-normal, captions, attributes
- Latent Structural Diffusion Model: denoise RGB, depth, normal together; replicated expert branches; spatial alignment; improved noise schedule; same timestep per branch
- Structure-Guided Refiner: compose predicted conditions, high resolution; robust conditioning against error accumulation
- Contributions: 1) framework + HumanVerse, early foundation model attempt; 2) Latent Structural Diffusion Model + Refiner; 3) state-of-the-art results

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Generating hyper-realistic human images from user conditions, e.g., text and pose, is very important for various applications, like image animation and virtual try-on. So many efforts have explored the task of controllable human image generation. Early methods either use variational auto-encoders (VAEs) in a reconstruction manner, or improve realism using generative adversarial networks (GANs). Some of them create high-quality images, but the unstable training and limited model capacity restrict them to small datasets with low diversity. The recent emergence of diffusion models (DMs) set a new paradigm for realistic synthesis, and they have become the predominant architecture in Generative AI. However, exemplar text-to-image (T2I) models like Stable Diffusion and DALL·E 2 still have trouble creating human images with coherent anatomy, e.g., arms and legs, and natural poses. The main reason is that a human is articulated with non-rigid deformations, and this needs structural information that text prompts can hardly describe.

To get structural control for image generation, recent works like ControlNet and T2I-Adapter add a learnable branch that modulates the pre-trained DMs, e.g., Stable Diffusion, in a plug-and-play manner. But these approaches suffer from feature discrepancy between the main branch and the auxiliary branch, which leads to inconsistency between the control signals (e.g., pose maps) and the generated images. To address this, HumanSD inputs the body skeleton directly into the diffusion U-Net by channel-wise concatenation. However it is limited to generating artistic style images with limited diversity. Also, human images are synthesized only with pose control, and other structural information like depth maps and surface-normal maps is not considered. In short, previous studies either take one control signal as input condition, or they treat different control signals separately as independent guidance, instead of modeling the multi-level correlations between human appearance and the different types of structural information. Realistic human generation with coherent structure is still unsolved.

In this paper we propose a unified framework, HyperHuman, to generate in-the-wild human images with high realism and diverse layouts. The key insight is that a human image is inherently structural over multiple granularities, from the coarse-level body skeleton to the fine-grained spatial geometry. So capturing these correlations between the explicit appearance and the latent structure in one model is essential to generate coherent and natural human images. First, we build a large-scale human-centric dataset called HumanVerse, with 340 M in-the-wild human images of high quality and diversity. It has comprehensive annotations, like the coarse-level body skeletons, the fine-grained depth and surface-normal maps, and the high-level image captions and attributes. Based on this, we design two modules for hyper-realistic controllable human image generation. In the Latent Structural Diffusion Model, we augment the pre-trained diffusion backbone so that it denoises the RGB, depth, and normal at the same time. We pick appropriate network layers to replicate as structural expert branches, so the model can handle input/output of different domains and also guarantee the spatial alignment between the denoised textures and structures. Because of this design, the image appearance, spatial relationship, and geometry are modeled jointly in a unified network, where each branch complements the others with both structural awareness and textural richness. To generate monotonous depth and surface-normal, which have similar values in local regions, we use an improved noise schedule to eliminate low-frequency information leakage. We sample the same timestep for each branch to get better learning and feature fusion. Then in the Structure-Guided Refiner we compose the predicted conditions, using the spatially-aligned structure maps, for detailed generation at high resolution. We also design a robust conditioning scheme to reduce the effect of error accumulation in our two-stage generation pipeline.

In summary, our main contributions are three-fold: 1) We propose a new HyperHuman framework for in-the-wild controllable human image generation with high realism. We curate a large-scale human-centric dataset, HumanVerse, with comprehensive annotations like human pose, depth, and surface normal. It is one of the earliest attempts at a human generation foundation model, and we hope it benefits future research. 2) We propose the Latent Structural Diffusion Model to jointly capture image appearance, spatial relationship, and geometry in a unified framework. We also devise the Structure-Guided Refiner to compose the predicted conditions for generation with better visual quality and higher resolution. 3) Extensive experiments show that HyperHuman gets state-of-the-art performance and generates hyper-realistic human images in diverse scenarios.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Generating hyper-realistic human images from user conditions, e.g., text and pose, is of great importance to various applications, such as image animation [1] and virtual try-on [2]. To this end, many efforts explore the task of controllable human image generation. Early methods either resort to variational auto-encoders (VAEs) in a reconstruction manner [3], or improve realism with generative adversarial networks (GANs) [4]. Though some of them create high-quality images [5,6], unstable training and limited model capacity confine them to small datasets of low diversity. The recent emergence of diffusion models (DMs) [7] has set a new paradigm for realistic synthesis, and DMs have become the predominant architecture in Generative AI [8]. Nevertheless, exemplar text-to-image (T2I) models like Stable Diffusion [9] and DALL·E 2 [10] still struggle to create human images with coherent anatomy, e.g., arms and legs, and natural poses. The main reason is that the human body is articulated with non-rigid deformations, requiring structural information that can hardly be depicted by text prompts.

To enable structural control for image generation, recent works like ControlNet [11] and T2I-Adapter [12] introduce a learnable branch to modulate the pre-trained DMs, e.g., Stable Diffusion, in a plug-and-play manner. However, these approaches suffer from feature discrepancy between the main and auxiliary branches, leading to inconsistency between the control signals (e.g., pose maps) and the generated images. To address this issue, HumanSD [13] proposes to directly input the body skeleton into the diffusion U-Net by channel-wise concatenation. However, it is confined to generating artistic style images of limited diversity. Besides, human images are synthesized only with pose control, while other structural information like depth maps and surface-normal maps is not considered. In a nutshell, previous studies either take a single control signal as input condition, or treat different control signals separately as independent guidance, instead of modeling the multi-level correlations between human appearance and different types of structural information. Realistic human generation with coherent structure remains unsolved.

In this paper, we propose a unified framework, HyperHuman, to generate in-the-wild human images of high realism and diverse layouts. The key insight is that a human image is inherently structural over multiple granularities, from the coarse-level body skeleton to fine-grained spatial geometry. Therefore, capturing such correlations between the explicit appearance and latent structure in one model is essential to generate coherent and natural human images. Specifically, we first establish a large-scale human-centric dataset called HumanVerse that contains 340 M in-the-wild human images of high quality and diversity. It has comprehensive annotations, such as coarse-level body skeletons, fine-grained depth and surface-normal maps, and high-level image captions and attributes. Based on this, two modules are designed for hyper-realistic controllable human image generation. In the Latent Structural Diffusion Model, we augment the pre-trained diffusion backbone to simultaneously denoise the RGB, depth, and normal. Appropriate network layers are chosen to be replicated as structural expert branches, so that the model can both handle input/output of different domains and guarantee the spatial alignment among the denoised textures and structures. Thanks to this design, the image appearance, spatial relationship, and geometry are jointly modeled within a unified network, where the branches complement each other with both structural awareness and textural richness. To generate monotonous depth and surface-normal that have similar values in local regions, we use an improved noise schedule to eliminate low-frequency information leakage. The same timestep is sampled for each branch to achieve better learning and feature fusion. With the spatially-aligned structure maps, in the Structure-Guided Refiner we compose the predicted conditions for detailed generation at high resolution. Moreover, we design a robust conditioning scheme to mitigate the effect of error accumulation in our two-stage generation pipeline.

To summarize, our main contributions are three-fold: 1) We propose a novel HyperHuman framework for in-the-wild controllable human image generation of high realism. A large-scale human-centric dataset, HumanVerse, is curated with comprehensive annotations like human pose, depth, and surface normal. As one of the earliest attempts at a human generation foundation model, we hope it will benefit future research. 2) We propose the Latent Structural Diffusion Model to jointly capture the image appearance, spatial relationship, and geometry in a unified framework. The Structure-Guided Refiner is further devised to compose the predicted conditions for generation of better visual quality and higher resolution. 3) Extensive experiments demonstrate that HyperHuman yields state-of-the-art performance, generating hyper-realistic human images under diverse scenarios.
